scenes.title: Highland stone reaches a coastal fishing community
scenes.body: People at Quebrada Jaguay used obsidian from the Alca highlands while living by the Pacific coast. The volcanic glass connects an early fishing settlement with inland stone sources.
scenes.note: Seasonal movement by the same people and exchange with highland communities are both possible. Do not assign every specimen to Alca-1 or depict a regular trading service. The broad early publication window is retained rather than mixing later stratigraphic recalibrations.

scenes.title: The California islands connect with the interior
scenes.body: Eight small obsidian pieces at a San Miguel Island shell-midden site match the West Sugarloaf source in the inland Coso volcanic field. Their site context places this material connection thousands of years before the large later shell-bead industries.
scenes.note: The site's 6440–6270 cal BP chronology is contextual. Surface collection does not establish the date of each piece. Exchange through successive communities is an interpretation; no particular mainland trail or sea crossing is recovered.

scenes.title: Lake Titicaca communities draw on distant toolstone
scenes.body: Tool makers at Jiskairumoko obtained obsidian from Chivay, west of Lake Titicaca. Two independent X-ray fluorescence methods assigned 66 of 68 excavated tools to that source.
scenes.note: The study dates the sampled occupation broadly, not each transfer. Its two unresolved specimens are not mapped to Alca. Consistent procurement does not identify a road, a merchant group, or whether people visited the source themselves.

scenes.title: Pacific shell reaches the upper Amazon
scenes.body: People at Santa Ana–La Florida placed fragments of a marine Strombus shell with the dead. The shell carried a Pacific coastal material into the upper Mayo–Chinchipe basin east of the Andes.
scenes.note: The coastal gathering place and intermediaries are unknown. This regional line does not prove a direct trans-Andean journey, a cacao return cargo, or a named coastal partner. Table 1's unusually narrow printed calibration for Beta-197176 is not treated as a ten-year transfer date.

scenes.title: Carnelian connects South Asia and Mesopotamia
scenes.body: Carnelian necklace beads at Kish have geochemical and manufacturing affinities with western India.
scenes.note: Fifteen analysed beads match the Deccan geological region; overlapping deposits prevent an exact quarry assignment. Raw stone or partly finished objects may have moved, with some bead manufacture in Mesopotamia.

scenes.title: Stone crosses the northeastern Caribbean
scenes.body: Visitors to Plum Piece on Saba worked flint brought from Long Island off Antigua. Flakes and prepared cores helped supply a camp whose occupants collected land crabs and seabirds.
scenes.note: Source assignment is the excavation team's lithic assessment, not a chemical match of every flake. The journey and intermediate islands are unknown. The paper’s seasonal-camp and canoe-making interpretations do not establish a sailing timetable.

scenes.title: San Lorenzo receives toolstone from different directions
scenes.body: San Lorenzo households used obsidian brought from El Chayal in Guatemala. The source appears in the earliest sampled phase and later supplied both flake-making stone and finished blades. San Lorenzo residents received obsidian nodules from the Guadalupe Victoria region of Puebla and struck them into cutting flakes. This nearer source supplied much of the community’s early toolstone.
scenes.note: Chemical source matches do not establish a direct itinerary. The period spans separately sampled phases, not a measured flow rate; the earliest phase has only a small El Chayal component. The line represents a source district and consumption district. Routes and intermediaries are unknown; this early phase record does not claim the source stopped supplying San Lorenzo after 1400 BCE.

scenes.title: Stone bowls move through the eastern woodlands
scenes.body: People at Poverty Point used soapstone bowls brought already carved from the southern Appalachian foothills. Broken vessels sometimes bear repair holes, showing that imported containers were maintained as useful possessions.
scenes.note: The source region is broad and the itinerary unknown. The nomination explicitly says there is no surviving evidence for what Poverty Point people supplied in return. The map does not assert travel along a particular river or continuous shipments across the whole occupation.

scenes.title: A ship carries a cargo of copper
scenes.body: Cypriot copper travelled in bulk aboard the ship lost off Uluburun.
scenes.note: The wreck is a cargo find, not a receiving market. Copper origin does not prove loading on Cyprus; the excavator considers a Levantine entrepôt likely. No destination or intermediate calls are asserted.

scenes.title: An early Copán household obtains obsidian
scenes.body: An early house at Las Sepulturas in the Copán Valley contained 74 obsidian pieces assigned to Ixtepeque. Residents made flake tools from imported nodules or large pieces of stone.
scenes.note: This is the excavated house assemblage, not the mixed Los Higos sample. Source assignment is visual in the reported table; direct procurement and successive exchanges are alternatives. Phase dates are broader than the single associated charcoal result.

scenes.title: Teouma participates in several island connections
scenes.body: Teouma residents used New Britain obsidian;25 Kutau/Bao pieces occur in Layer 3 burial fills and midden. Two Vanua Lava obsidian flakes occur in Teouma Layer 3, documenting movement within Vanuatu. A Gaua obsidian flake in Teouma’s Layer 3 midden connects the Banks Islands with southern Efate.
scenes.note: Settlement-era transport and exchange overlap. Later disturbed pieces are excluded.

scenes.title: New Britain obsidian reaches northern Borneo
scenes.body: Cutting flakes at Bukit Tengkorak include obsidian traced to Kutau/Bao in New Britain, over 3,000 km away.
scenes.note: No direct voyage is established. The older unidentified obsidian group is excluded.

scenes.title: Pottery moves through Torres Strait
scenes.body: An early pot fragment at Ormi has temper pointing to western Torres Strait, rather than Dauar’s local geology.
scenes.note: Mua, Dauan and Mabaduan remain alternative sources. Transport is established; trade and migration are not separable.

scenes.title: Taiwan jade in the northern Philippines
scenes.body: Anaro craftspeople cut and drilled imported Taiwan nephrite into ornaments, sometimes recycling older tools. A jade ear ornament beside a burial jar at Savidug was made from Fengtian nephrite.
scenes.note: This interval does not date all surface finds. Source geology does not identify a departure port. Layer dates deposition, not manufacture. The separate unstratified production discard is excluded.

scenes.title: Pepper crosses the Indian Ocean
scenes.body: A Berenike storage jar contained over 7.5 kg of black pepper, material evidence for Indian Ocean spice exchange.
scenes.note: The jar's context dates the deposition, not harvesting or sailing. Southern India is a broad source inference from the plant and trade evidence; no Malabar port is uniquely proved.

scenes.title: Silk reaches a Palmyra tomb
scenes.body: A silk textile from Palmyra Tomb 40 is catalogued as Chinese silk.
scenes.note: The catalogue's AD 100 is an approximate object date, not an exact shipment year. China is a broad production attribution; this item does not establish a single caravan route or an uninterrupted trade duration.

scenes.title: Coastal shell reaches the inland East Bay
scenes.body: An Olivella saucer bead found at Santa Rita in the inland East Bay has an isotope signature consistent with southern California shell. Its direct date of about 333–476 CE provides an early anchor for northward coastal material movement.
scenes.note: The authors describe regional isotope separation as tentative and leave some specimens unassigned. This bead cannot identify a particular island workshop or the path by which it reached Pleasanton. Its shell age may precede final deposition.

scenes.title: California islanders obtain eastern Sierra obsidian
scenes.body: A projectile point from San Miguel Island was made from Casa Diablo obsidian, far inland near the eastern Sierra Nevada. Its site dates to approximately 470–830 CE, showing that island communities obtained stone from more than one inland source.
scenes.note: The chronological interval dates the site association. It does not identify a named trader, a regular service, or the number of hands through which the stone passed.

scenes.title: Georgia vessels enter Florida ceremonial contexts
scenes.body: Cooking vessels made near Georgia’s lower Altamaha River reached burial mounds along Florida’s lower St. Johns. Chemical composition, clay comparisons and some matching stamped designs connect everyday pots with ceremonies farther down the Atlantic coast.
scenes.note: The plotted endpoints represent regions. A matching paddle design alone cannot distinguish a moving pot from a moving paddle; the compositional evidence supplies the stronger connection. Gift exchange during ceremonies is the authors’ interpretation, not a documented transaction.

scenes.title: Caribbean communities exchange stone for axes
scenes.body: People at Golden Rock made axes from St. Martin greenstone. Finished axes, preforms, and stoneworking debris show that material crossed between islands and was worked at the receiving settlement.
scenes.note: The source is a distributed geological formation. The finds demonstrate movement of stone, but they cannot identify every voyage or separate direct collection from exchange. Other locally worked rocks are not assigned to St. Martin.

scenes.title: Stone moves within southeastern Australia
scenes.body: A quartzite flake and a later hornfels flake from ground-edge tools at MR/1 match Nepean–Grose and Yarramundi river-gravel samples.
scenes.note: Sample locations are not exact extraction points. Direct procurement and exchange cannot be separated.

scenes.title: Glass connects African and European workshops to eastern production
scenes.body: Beads placed in Komani graves include glass traced to Mesopotamian production. Glass from the eastern Islamic world reached Gao Saney, where imported drawn tubes could be cut into beads.
scenes.note: This link selects the Mesopotamian soda-ash group, excluding the distinct cold-cut beads and reused natron glass. A specific production centre and chain of merchants remain unidentified. Group 1 chemistry suggests Iraq, Iran or northern Syria, probably Iraq. The selected contexts precede the later source shift. Cross-Saharan and Sahelian itineraries cannot be resolved from the glass alone.

scenes.title: Cloves reach a Sri Lankan port
scenes.body: A clove found at Mantai shows an eastern spice reaching this Sri Lankan port.
scenes.note: Maluku is the plant's native range, not a chemically identified orchard. Intermediary cultivation or transshipment is possible; the source-to-find line does not imply a direct voyage. The clove is dated by its layer.

scenes.title: Chaco receives shell from Pacific and Gulf waters
scenes.body: People at a Chaco Canyon village used black abalone shell for pendants. Two excavated examples connect the village with the Pacific California–Baja California coast in contexts dated 900–1040 CE. Shell pendants from Chaco village 29SJ627 belong to a marine-shell tradition that the excavation synthesis links to the Gulf of California. People worked and wore imported shell alongside other ornaments in the canyon.
scenes.note: The species identifies a broad Pacific source range. It does not isolate Alta California, the Channel Islands, a workshop, a direct journey to Chaco, or goods sent in return. The Gulf endpoint follows the published regional interpretation. These individual pendants lack isotope sourcing, and the broader Mexican Pacific distribution of related shell taxa prevents an exact collection locality from being claimed. No reciprocal traffic or direct expedition is demonstrated.

scenes.title: Merchants bring tropical goods to imperial Mexico
scenes.body: Merchants returned from Xicalanco to Mexico with goods obtained for Ahuitzotl and presented them to the ruler. The account records royal procurement through long-distance merchants.
scenes.note: Book 9's retrospective narrative identifies the patron and endpoints, but supplies no exact departure, itinerary or shipment date here. The connection does not classify Xicalanco as a tribute province or infer a maritime leg. Individual goods are not reconstructed from the incomplete adjoining-folio view.

scenes.title: Inka stone moves north from the Cusco region
scenes.body: Worked andesite blocks recovered around Paquishapa in the Saraguro basin chemically match Rumiqolqa near Cusco. The movement carried imperial building material far north into present-day Ecuador.
scenes.note: XRF supports the source-to-find connection, not a complete road itinerary. Reused stones need not stand at their original building. Huayna Capac's reign is the author's most likely attribution, not a precisely dated haul; alternatives include earlier reigns and the years before 1532. Proposed final delivery to Tomebamba is not mapped as an observed endpoint.

scenes.title: State maize moves through Andean storage and transport
scenes.body: Maize grown on Inca state lands in Cochabamba was collected at Paria. Sora herders of Sipe-Sipe managed this transport, using llamas and labor organized through imperial obligations. Paria served as a collecting and storage center before Cochabamba maize was carried onward to Cusco. The two legs describe one documented imperial redistribution chain.
scenes.note: This is state production and redistribution, not a private market route. The start is a rounded historical period and 1525 is a reign bound, not a last shipment. Maize also supported workers locally; not every harvest left the valley. The disputed historic Paria geography is represented by a regional anchor. This second leg is linked to the Cochabamba–Paria record, not independent proof of a second commodity network. No road geometry, intermediate depot, shipment volume or regular timetable is inferred. Reign and period bounds are approximate; continuation after 1525 is unresolved.

scenes.title: Tribute concentrates food and materials in Tenochtitlan
scenes.body: Soconusco communities owed cacao and drinking vessels to the Aztec capital. The connection represents compulsory tribute recorded for the province. The Tochtepec province delivered rubber balls, cacao and woven garments as tribute. Its named towns formed a major collecting district on the southern Gulf side. Tochpan's Gulf-coast province supplied garments, featherwork and dried chilies to imperial Mexico through tribute obligations. Cuauhnahuac's tribute included paper, gourds and cloth. These deliveries linked communities south of the Basin of Mexico to the imperial collecting system.
scenes.note: The manuscript was compiled after conquest. The plotted year is a labelled approximate pre-conquest snapshot, not an exact shipment date or proof of the system's onset. Provincial goods may have been acquired from other producers. Quantities and delivery frequencies are omitted where glosses and scholarly readings differ. The manuscript was compiled after conquest. Quantities and delivery frequencies are omitted where glosses and scholarly readings differ. Paper units are especially ambiguous; no precise sheet count is asserted.
